utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday. Good morning to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Praljak, and good morning to the other three accused who are not in the courtroom for reasons -- at least for two of them, for health reasons. Good morning to the Defence counsel. Good morning Mr. Stringer, and my very good morning to all the people assisting us. Mr. Karnavas, the Registrar told us that you have used up, so far, one hour and 33 minutes. The Trial Chamber would like to know how much time you will need to finish with your cross-examination, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. I can safely say that the remainder of my time will not be enough. However, I will do my very -- my level best to complete my cross-examination within the four hours the Trial Chamber has allotted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, do try to give short answers, because I had the same problem; I thought that it would take me only two or three days to put all my questions to you, but in fact it took almost six days. So I think that Mr. Karnavas may be faced with the same difficulty as I had. Do make an effort to provide short answers, all the more so, Mr. Praljak, since you know that the Judges, but also the Prosecutor and all the Defence counsel, have a good grasp -- maybe not as good as yours, but a good grasp of the case. We know quite a lot about the case, so that you can really go to the crux of the matter when you answer, and the Judges, the Defence counsel, can then ask questions that otherwise they would have been able to because you provided too long answers before. But I know you do your level best. But left us aim for efficiency, all of us. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, General Praljak. Let's pick up where we left yesterday, just a few questions left on --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- on this particular document, which is 1D03 -- 1D03141 is the document. And for you, the page number is going to be -- look at 1815.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all the microphones not in use please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you found it, sir? Let me repeat. We're on document 1D03141, and for you, if you look at the page, the bottom, you'll see "1D51-1815." And it will be page 4 for those who are looking at the English version. And over here, it talks about that when Alija Izetbegovic was president of the Presidency, at that period of time, that there was an effort to get certain individuals that were arrested to be put in prison and to have criminal proceedings launched against them, and an individual by the name of Bakir Alispahic refused. Do you know who Bakir Alispahic is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who is he, or who was he at the time, what positions he held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the secret services at the time, the Muslim secret services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we clarify the time-frame, whether it's 1996, which is the article, or whether it's during an earlier period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If some patience is exercised, I will go to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand the technique behind the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Why must the answer be delayed, Mr. Karnavas? I do not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, usually you ask a question, you get an answer, you ask a question, you get an answer. The question was -- he told me who he was. The follow-up question, which I didn't have an opportunity to respond -- forgive me for being aggressive, but it seems that I'm coming under attack by the Prosecution and you now. I had asked who the general was. The next logical question would have been, At what period of time? So if everybody exercised a little bit of patience, I'm get to it. I would certainly appreciate a little courtesy from everybody around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us at what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I do not think that you're very well qualified to ask for courtesy, and it would have been courteous to answer the question, which is an innocent question, I would say. I do not understand this, but we've lost enough time now. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because my integrity is coming under attack by you personally now, given your remarks. Now, I asked who the gentleman was, I wasn't given an opportunity to ask at what period of time, because the gentleman held several positions and we'll see his name on earlier occasions. We know what period of time this document makes reference to. So I would ask that you be a little bit patient. And I understand that there is a great deal of animosity towards me. I understand that, Your Honour. But I'm trying to be professional -- as professional as I possibly can be; perhaps not to your likings, but that's what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, at what period of time did this gentleman hold the position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he came to that position as the head of the AID, the Muslim secret services, after the murder of Nedzad Ugljen in 1993 or 1994, sometime up to 1996, when he was removed. He was removed in 1996, and approximately one or two years before -- actually, I can't be sure exactly of the time when he was appointed, but I know that he succeeded Nedzad Ugljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we'll see that name --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll be seeing that name again. Now, if we go further down the page, you would see that someone is quoted as saying: "I don't know" -- this is a Munir Alibabic, he says: "I don't know why the Americans act so naively. They should have seen what happened to us." And he says this in November 1997. Alibabic also explains that he was forced to resign: "Because he was resisting the Iranian influence in the Bosnian agency." The article says that Alibabic's view was shared by Nedzad Ugljen and Nedzad Herenda, as well as the fact that the author of the text spoke with five more employees of the AID. Do you know who Nedzad Herenda was? Do you know of him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name does ring a bell, in the same context with Nedzad Ugljen, who was murdered to be prevented from telling what was going on in Sarajevo. Nedzad Herenda was in the top echelon of the secret services of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, to be more precise, of the secret service of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we see further down in the text that at one point the Presidency, which included Kljujic, Komsic, Ganic, they were informed about certain activities by Alibabic. They accused him of unlawful activities in the services, usurping the competencies, nepotism, drug smuggling, intercepting Presidency members and high officials in the government, espionage for foreign intelligence services, lack of professionalism, and so on. This is in the following page, sir. It would be on 1816, if you look at the following page. And then it goes on, at the very last part of the paragraph: "The most interesting part of the public was that the one about intercepts, for the sake of the truth, and the then president of the Presidency found that part most interesting because it was found out then that the services at the time, when Alibabic was the head of the Sarajevo Sector, of the SDB, with the consent of Alija Izetbegovic, was intercepting Fikret Abdic and Miro Lasic." Can you think of any reason why Izetbegovic would want to be listening in and intercepting conversations of Fikret Abdic and Miro Lasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just for the record, and then I won't intervene anymore, just continue the objection from yesterday about the relevance of this line of questioning. And then, more specifically, the question here, it assumes that this article from this publication, actually, is correct, which may or may not be, but to take assertions and to sort of take for granted that they're correct and then ask the witness to comment is sort of an extra leap that I think goes, to the very least, at the probative value, if not the relevance. So having said that, Mr. President, I'll try to avoid intervening on relevancy grounds further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday, we heard that Miro Lasic was one of the individuals that Alija Izetbegovic did not want -- prevented from attending negotiations in Geneva. Fikret Abdic, first of all, I believe the President asked questions regarding this particular individual, and so -- and it's no secret that he was an elected official, that he was in the Presidency. We heard from Franjo Boris about Mr. Abdic. And as we will see later on today, there are reasons why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But can you think of any reason why the president -- assuming that this is correct, why Izetbegovic would want to intercept members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am very sure about the reasons. Fikret Abdic was the most popular politician among the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the first free elections. He gained the most number of voters by far. But it is very clear, and I know that the team of Young Muslims who joined the SDA made it sure to throw out Fikret Abdic from the political game completely, because he opted for totally different political options. He was a Muslim, but he advocated a secular society, a democratic society, and Fikret Abdic didn't care too much about that, and he also didn't care too much about the positions of Lasic. And it is more than likely that he intercepted them for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the bottom of page 5, at the very last sentence, it begins, and it goes on to page 6, and it may be further down the next page for you, General Praljak, it says: "According to the latest finding of the investigation, identities of all Bosnians arrested during the IFOR air drop have been charged and the trainees were not practicing how to catch war criminals only, but also how to hunt down and liquidate opposition and disobeying politicians, including academician Muhamed Filipovic, Sefer Halilovic, Alija Delimustafic, Miro Lazovic, and Adil Zulfikarpasic. Now, yesterday we talked about Mr. Halilovic and there was an objection. Do you know whether Mr. Halilovic was the target of an attack and whether his family -- members of his family were killed? Do you know --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know that, and I also know that there was a special unit under the control of the top echelon of the SDA, under the name Seva, and that group went around Sarajevo killing Muslims which were not suitable, as well as Serbs and Croats, and this was done mostly by snipers. And that group comprised of four members of the former Yugoslav Shooting Team. And that group was led by Nedzad Ugljen, and that group made an attempt at Sefer Halilovic's life, but they made a mistake. They mistook his brother-in-law for him, and that's how it came that they killed a wrong person and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we'll get to that. We'll see more proof of that later. But going on, this is what Izetbegovic had to say when confronted with this information. He said: "Yes, I know of Alispahic's contact with the Iranians. Alispahic was contacting not only Iranians, but also, as far as I know, America, British, and French intelligence services. He was the minister of the interior for a long time and the head of AID for a number of years." Now, do you know about what period of time Alispahic would have been the minister of interior? And if you don't know, there's no need to speculate. We'll --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was before the war. I really can't be sure. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally with this document, at the very end he's asked about -- Izetbegovic was asked a number of questions, and his answer is: "I did not know of the Pogorelica camp. I heard about it in Rome when the media reported about SFOR entering the camp." Now, how is it possible that this camp could be operating with all of these services, conducting all of these affairs, with agencies that are under Izetbegovic's control, and he not know about this camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible, it's absolutely impossible. 50 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina knew about that camp. It was almost a public secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to switch to -- we're going to go back to something else that we started yesterday because of some concerns that we have on the Defence concerning the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We're going to go back -- we're going to look at a map, and that's 1D02843. And I'm going to go back to page 86 from yesterday, because Judge Trechsel asked the question, and the question was, on line 8: "I'm quite aware of how complicated matters were ethnically, but on the list of municipalities forming the HZ-HB, they do not figure, do they, in the list of 18 November 1991?" Now, I don't want to waste too much of my time on this matter, but if we could go through some documents very quickly, perhaps we could answer some of those questions, though I believe we have answered those questions previously. If we look at the map first, just look at it. Now I'm going to turn to Exhibit 1D02255, 1D02255, and if you have that with you, and I'm going to read, and we could look at the dates as well. That might help us. It says here "20 August 1992." This is in regards to Usora, and it states: "Based on the initiative of Herceg-Bosna HZ Croatian Community for all Croatian communities to join the single community of Herceg-Bosna in Bosnia and Herzegovina, while expressing the will of the Croatian people, at the meeting held on 20th August 1992, the Usora HZ Assembly adopted the following:" And we can see a decision was adopted: "A decision is hereby adopted for Usora to join Herceg-Bosna HZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And could you please -- now, yesterday we went through the map, because this goes to this whole notion of Banovina and the Prosecution's intent on having borders drawn around Herceg-Bosna. If we could look at the map very quickly, and maybe you can look at Usora, and you told us that it was a very small place. Can we switch back to the map, please. It's 1D02843. That's the map. Okay. Now, we covered it yesterday, but I'm going to eat up a little more time just to clear up this matter, hopefully once and for all. Where is Usora? We have it there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this Croatian Community in Usora, was it setting up borders, as in geographical borders, maybe with a wall separating, you know, the Croats from the Serbs and the Muslims, like they do in some countries where they have a wall separating the borders, be it the American-Mexican border? Is that -- so do we have a border over there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now let's go to the next document, which is 1D02252, 1D02252. You can leave the map up there. If you don't have the -- you have the document physically, but we --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at this. This is 19th August 1992. 19 August 1992: "Pursuant to Article 5 of the statutory decision on temporary establishment of the executive authorities, the Presidency of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Central Bosnia, at the session held on 19 August 1992, adopted the following ..." This is a decision, and I'm going to read part of it: "On the basis of and in keeping with the will of the representatives of the Croatian people of the Croatian Community of Central Bosnia, the region of the municipalities of Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj, and Teslic shall hereby join the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. With the act of accession of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, all regulations adopted at the level of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be valid in the joint territories of the community." Now, by this decision, General Praljak, were they setting up borders, connecting all of these municipalities, to somehow carve out this area so it could be part of some sort of an annexed portion to go to Croatia or to ethnically cleanse the Muslims from the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us -- can you mark -- can you find those municipalities and mark them here, the areas? And maybe if you can, tell us exactly which areas in those municipalities of Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj, and Teslic were the Croats located, because the impression some have in this court, even after three years, is that they took the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could we have an IC number for this document, Mr. President, so we can move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be given Exhibit IC01033. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these municipalities, Croats were a minority. They lived in some of the areas of these municipalities. And faced with the aggression, which was visible, faced with the lack of organisation among the central government to defend themselves, they organised themselves under the laws that were in place at the moment. Parts of the municipalities, local communes and some other things, were allowed to join in a wider organisation in order to defend themselves, and that is the sense of what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, we're going to move to a separate -- another topic, and now we're going to be focusing primarily on Izetbegovic, and we're going to be going through some documents. But first I want to refer to your testimony at page 40260. You were asked some questions, and at some point you said the following. And I'm just saying this as a way of background: "I gained the impression," referring to Izetbegovic, "I have a very good opinion of him as a human being. As a man, however, I do claim and agree with what Mr. Filipovic says in his book. The leadership, and that's what Filipovic says in his book, Izetbegovic wasn't the leader. It was Cengic Senior and Cengic Junior, and the people around him, Omerbegovic and so on. And whatever they didn't like, they would change. If they didn't like something, he had decided they would change the decision." Now, that's what Mr. Filipovic writes about, and you seem to agree with Mr. Filipovic. Now I'm going to go through a series of documents, or portions of a couple of documents, and perhaps then ask you whether you still maintain that Mr. Filipovic may be correct, because I will put to you at the end that Izetbegovic was in fact the leader, was in fact in full control, was in fact the one calling all of the decisions, and was in fact pursuing his Islamic Declaration; that is, setting up an Islamic country in Bosnia-Herzegovina, be it in part or in whole. So I'm going to put to you, after we go through some documents. And with that, I'm going to refer you to -- we're going to start off with portions of the document that we have -- from the book "Unholy Terror." And the number is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The number of the document is 1D03137, and we're going to go through portions of this, so I just -- and we'll also be covering the Islamic Declaration. If we can focus on page 72, page 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have a special binder with the entire document, so you won't have to -- you can just use that, and I'll make references to the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Praljak, it would be 1873. Those are the -- 1872 and 1873. Those are the pages, those are the last four digits of the number, 1872, going into 1873. So if you follow along. And this part of my cross deals with Izetbegovic's character. We see -- we see that on page 72, the following is being reported: "Like most JNA generals, Kukanjac took a dim view of Izetbegovic, whom he regarded as an unpleasant chameleon with dangerous views, yet he had no choice but to deal with him. The military's perception of the SDA leader --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "... was neatly summarised by a former JNA officer. He was known as an extremist who was known from Tito's time. He was not taken seriously, even though he had served a jail sentence for nationalist activities. He undertook moves that the military leadership proclaimed unconstitutional and illegal. And then stop worrying about him. Yet it was perfectly clear that the only thing Alija Izetbegovic feared was the JNA." Now, if we go on to page 203, and I'll give you the page number, General Praljak. This book was recently published, as I understand, in Croatian. And so if you look at 1898, those would be the numbers on your page. And for us, it's page 203. We see here it says: "Many Muslims quietly agreed with Adil Zulfikarpasic's verdict, 'Izetbegovic is worst than the Muslim's worst enemy.' Peace, for its own sake, had limited appeal to the SDA leadership. They had willed a civil war with their aggressive political Islam and their refusal to take the rights of non-Muslims seriously." It goes further down to say, the next paragraph: "Even some of the president's closest confidantes were having doubts about his political abilities. Izetbegovic's carefully-crafted outwardly image -- other-worldly image, so effective with the Western media, grated on many SDA higher-ups who found his retreat into prayer and contemplation a hazard. 'Alija doesn't know what a state is,' stated Nazif Sacirbegovic, the president's longest-serving partner in Islam. 'He belongs in a mosque, not in a government,' he said in 1993. "Izetbegovic's political opponents were even more pointed, particularly the irrepressible Fikret Abdic, who denounced the president as, 'the cunning imposter and the biggest murderer of his own people.' 'Everybody now realises that Izetbegovic's goal is a Muslim state,' he explained in 1993, adding a sketch of the man based on his personal experience, 'Alija is again trying to remain a humble, nice man, the eternal loser, but behind the scenes we actually have his love of power and his life's dream of creating a state known only to himself, which he conceived in his mind while he was doing time in Foca Prison and writing his Islamic Declaration, which he has never renounced.'" Now, first of all, if I could ask you one question. We know who Mr. Abdic is. Adil Zulfikarpasic, I don't know whether you covered that to any degree, but do you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, we were never introduced, but I have been aware of his life and work from before the war, quite a long time -- well, are you interested in all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether you knew the gentleman. Is it not a fact that he was one of the founding fathers of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this fellow, Sacirbegovic, are you aware that his son at the time, who changed his name to Sacirbey, was also serving as the ambassador to the United States for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he served as ambassador to the US, and he is, in fact, an American citizen, just as Zulfikarpasic has Swiss citizenship. But just a correction. Well, you mentioned Omerbegovic when you were listing Alija Izetbegovic's associate. It is Omer Behmen, not Omerbegovic, so that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I want to switch to the "Islamic Declaration," just a couple of passages, and we're going to be going into that document to some degree. So if we look at the "Islamic Declaration," -- and, Your Honours, we have that in a separate binder for you as well. And for the record, this is 1D00431, and we start off with just the motto at the beginning: "Our goal: The Islamisation of Muslims. Our motto: Believe and struggle." And then we go on to page 4 in the English version. I'm just going to cover some bits and pieces of it. It will be 2 for you, sir, page 2. We see, in the second paragraph: "In this conviction, we announce to our friends and enemies alike the Muslims are determined to take their fate of the Islamic world into their own hand and arrange that world according to their own vision of it." He later on goes on to say: "Its novelty lies in that it seeks to promote ideas and plans to organise action. The struggle towards new goals did not begin today. On the contrary, it has already experienced jihada, and its history contains pages of the suffering of its victims. Still, this is mainly the personal sacrifice of exceptional individuals of courageous minor groups, in collision with the mighty forces of the jihalija." Those are the -- and we see they have translate -- definitions of them at the bottom of the page: "The magnitude of the problem and its difficulties, however, require the organised action of millions." Then if we go to page 28 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just a correction of the interpretation I received in Croatian. It was said that the Muslims are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology. This is impossible to back-translate into English. It's virtually one-and-the-same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it says here that the ideas and plans should be translated into organised action, and this was mistranslated. So this is just a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to go to another area of your testimony, and then -- because here again you make some assertions about Alija Izetbegovic. And you say on page 39.740, you say the following: "Alija may have thought that he would remain untouched in his position, et cetera. That can be understood, in a way. He was probably impressed. He was in fear for his own people, but certainly all those who were being attacked from his territory saw -- looked at that from another angle. And we asked him, Why didn't you do anything against that, the same way the citizens of Zagreb did, something against things they didn't like." Now, this was in an answer to a question that was posed to you, and again I'm going to be asking you later on about your impressions, because you seem to be giving Izetbegovic the benefit of the doubt, because then later on you go on to say again, and this is on page 40.258 of the transcript, again saying with Filipovic, you go back and say: "Alija Izetbegovic wasn't independent in making his decisions. He would make a decision, and then what would happen was that the party leadership, which included these individuals, these Young Muslims, they quite simply changed the decision. So what is important to see that, and it's important for Their Honours to understand, that's why he changed his decision so often." And then you talk a little bit about the Young Muslims. But isn't it a fact, sir, that Mr. Izetbegovic was a Young Muslim himself? He was a member of the Young Muslims during World War II, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was actually tried twice for his affiliation with the Young Muslims and for fomenting the ideas of the Young Muslims. Once, immediately after World War II, and the other time it was in 1983. In 1983, I was familiar with the trial. I followed it closely, and I also studied in-depth the "Islamic Declaration," which was printed -- the first printing run was 200.000 copies and it was widely available. So I was quite familiar with the whole movement. Mr. Karnavas, I'm speaking from the perspective of what I knew from my meetings and talks with Mr. Izetbegovic. He simply -- well, a decision would be made, and I am not aware of a single decision that he didn't change afterwards. So it was my logical conclusion -- was that somebody was somebody actually was running him. It's difficult to assume that somebody is able to look you in the eye and just lie all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But isn't it a fact, sir, that in the Islamic religion, there is the possibility where -- at least this is what some scholars are saying, that when it comes to the promotion of Islam, or if Islam comes under attack, the individual is permitted, in fact encouraged, to lie? Isn't that part of their own religious upbringing? And the term, I believe, and we're going to get to it later on, but it's called "takia."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I am relatively well acquainted with the Koran, and as any other religion, Islam has a number of interpretations. It can be interpreted in various ways. The holy book, the Koran, can be interpreted in various ways. For a long time when I lived in Mostar, I lived side-by-side with Muslims, so apart from the Young Muslims, in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, so before the influence of the hard-line Islam from outside, the view of the Muslims was quite different. I have to say that my friends, many friends that I have, and I still have them, simply did not interpret the Koran in the way in which it is interpreted in the other variants that come from Iran or Saudi Arabia. But it is true that the Young Muslims interpreted the Koran as excluding the possibility of any coexistence between Muslims and Christians; the real interpretation of the Koran was the identity that affected both you, as a citizen, and you, as a religious person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's look at -- I'll get ahead of myself a little bit. Let's look at the "Islamic Declaration," going back to 1D00431. It's page 25 in the English version. I'm going to be looking at page 25 and then on page 30. And we're going to be going back and forth on these two documents. For you, General, it would be 10, page 00010. It says at the bottom part of the page, the last paragraph -- the last part of the paragraph: "There's only one possible way out; the formation and grouping of a new intelligentsia which thinks and feels Islam. This intelligentsia would then fly the flag of the Islamic Order, and together with the Muslim masses, take action to bring it about." Then if we go to page 30 of the "Islamic Declaration," we don't have time to go through every passage, but if we go to page 30, and I'll give you the number real quickly, it's -- it would be page 12, it says there, sort of in the middle of the page: "First and foremost of these conclusions is certainly the incompatibility of Islam with non-Islamic systems. There can be neither peace nor coexistence between the Islamic religion and non-Islamic social and political institutions. The failure of these institutions to function in the instability of the regimes in Muslim countries manifest in frequent change and coup d'etat is most often the consequence of their a priori opposition to Islam as the fundamental and foremost feeling of the people in these countries. By claiming the right to order its own world itself, Islam obviously excludes the right or possibility of action on the part of any foreign ideology on the territory. There is, therefore, no lay principle and the state should both reflect and support religious moral concepts." Now, I'm not going to go on, but -- on this for right now, but isn't it a fact that Izetbegovic, immediately after coming out of prison, the first thing that he did was print copies of his "Islamic Declaration," and then pass them out at the SDA founding session, and copies were being printed and distributed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true, and it's a terrible, terrible text. There can be no doubt about it. I have said so many times. It reflects the political concept of Alija Izetbegovic and his circle. It is the most extreme and the most hard-line interpretation of the Koran of Islam. And the third point, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic never renounced the "Islamic Declaration." Well, it is quite natural. If you draft your philosophical world-view, and in 1993 Mr. Izetbegovic was, well, not an old man, but he was well advanced in years, it was not written by a child or a youth who would then be able to renounce the foolishness of his youth, the delusions. It is a terrible book, a very terrible book, and it had a great deal of political reverberations among Croats and Serbs, because you cannot live with people [as interpreted] like that. This is the "either/or" mathematical function, you or him, it cannot be both, so it is an exclusive interpretation, ruling out the possibility of coexistence. So there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to correct the mistake in the transcript. Page 22, line 21, the interpretation of Mr. Praljak was "you cannot live with people like that." And what the general said was "you cannot live with that." He did not mention "people" at all. The point is that you cannot live with this ideology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain once again. When this book was published, this brochure, this book, it was clear that it advocates -- that this book advocates certain positions; that it would be impossible to live together. The book claims that, We cannot go together. When we are there, you will not be there, and you will live under the laws of a completely religious state, the Sharia law and so on. And of course it caused a great deal of political upset, and then it spiralled into objections on the other side. People said, Well, if they want an Islamic -- a Muslim state, we cannot agree to that. So in addition to the Serb ideas where they had aspirations to territories that did not belong to them, these are the causes of the war. All the rest is just consequences. In chess parlance, it is forced moves. Once you do two moves, all the 15 moves that follow, follow from the initial two moves. So these are forced moves, and it all goes on from there, as I've explained to you, obeying the laws of nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, all right, we heard -- we heard your answer, but now let's go look at, again, back to the "Islamic Declaration," and perhaps this may give us some food for thought at some point. Page 24 in the English version, middle of the paragraph -- middle of the page, it says here: "By their acts," and this would be on page 0009 in your document, "By their acts, modernists have created a state of internal conflict and confusion in which any programme, Islamic or foreign, becomes impracticable. The masses want Islamic action, but cannot carry it through without the intelligentsia. An alienated intelligentsia imposes a programme --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it possible to have the reference again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 24. The interpreters should have both the English and the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You had said 34, and that's the problem. At least that's what the record says and where I was looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. Page 24, and we -- I have an extra hard copy if the interpreters would -- in English --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, we just wanted the page number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll start again: "By their acts, modernists have created a state of internal conflict and confusion in which any programme, Islamic or foreign, becomes impracticable. The masses want Islamic action, but cannot carry it through without the intelligentsia. An alienated intelligentsia imposes a programme, but cannot find enough people prepared to contribute blood, sweat and enthusiasm for this paper ideal. The opposing forces cancel each other out, and a state of powerlessness and paralysis sets in." Now, going back to what you were saying, because there is one reference where -- in the "Islamic Declaration," Mr. Praljak, as I'm sure you're aware of, where he talks about creating an Islamic federation from Morocco to Indonesia, from Tropical Africa to Central Asia. And then he says, on page 61, which in your document would be -- and I apologise for just having to do snippets of this, but I have time limitations. On page 61, which is in your document, it would be 0024. It says: "We find it, for instance, absolutely unacceptable and unreal that in this day and age of concentration and association, one people, Arabs, should be broken up into 13 units of states, that the Muslim states stand on opposite sides on a number of significant international questions, that Muslim Egypt is unconcerned about the sufferings of Muslims in Ethiopia or Kashmir. That is the height of confrontation of the Arab countries with Israel. Muslim Persia maintained friendly relations with the aggressor, et cetera. If anything is unreal, then it is not the unity of the Muslims, but its absence, the state of division and discord. In fact, we find it today." Now, let's just pause for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I mean that it is good to pause a bit. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's pause for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here we hear some passages from the intelligentsia. The Young Muslims, which Izetbegovic associated himself with, in forming the SDA, were they not the intellectuals, or some of the -- I'm not saying all of the intellectuals, but were they not, we call, part of the intelligentsia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here he's talking -- the second passage that I read, he bemoans the fact that, for instance, Egypt is unconcerned about the Muslims in Ethiopia and Kashmir, and of course during this period of time when he was writing, and even today, there's conflict. Was it not a fact that the Mujahedin, these Islamic fighters, came from such countries in order to help their Muslim brothers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the Islamic cause, I should say, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the reason why they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to what Mr. Schindler has to say in "The Unholy Terror," and that's 1D03137, and we're going to look at page 36. And I'll give you the number in Croatian right now, it's 1843 -- 1842-1843, those are the digits that have you to look at. At the very top, we see: "The Young Muslims were collaborators with the Nazis from the beginning of the Bosnia's occupation in 1941. They provided the Gestapo with lists of 'progressive' students of Belgrade University, many of whom were arrested, even killed, for suspected pro-Communism." Then we go all the way to the bottom, last paragraph: "Despite its modest fighting powers, the Handzar Division had succeeded in tarring the Bosnian Muslims with the taint of collaboration with the occupiers, specifically enthusiastic cooperation with the SS. While it is unfair to place blame for this on all Bosnian Muslims, there was ample liability in the case of the Muslim religious establishment and especially with Islamist groups such as the Young Muslims. As the tied of the war turned decisively against the Germans in 1944, and the Wehrmacht commenced a gradual retreat out of the Balkans, those who had collaborated with the Nazis and Ustashas faced a bleak future. It was only in the last months of the war that the Muslims joined Tito's Partisan forces in any numbers, and that was mainly because the Communists enforced conscriptions in liberated areas which, by the end of 1944, included most of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In brackets: "(Among the less-than-willing soldiers in Partisan uniform in the last months of the war were the Young Muslim activists Alija Izetbegovic and Nazif Sacirbegovic)." So it was a fact that he was a Young Muslim, correct, Alija himself, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that he had been in prison for that. Now let's look at page 39 of the same document, which is 1D00431 for the record, and you will be looking, sir, at page number -- the last four digits are 1846. For us in English, it is page 39. It says: "The Young Muslims found life under Communist uncongenial - not least because some of its members were in prison or wanted for collaboration with the Nazis - but they continued their activities clandestinely. One of their major accomplishments was the publication of their journal, 'El Mujahid (The Holy Warrior),' whose first edition displayed unmistakable signs of Pan-Islamist radicalism: Calls for jihad, ample Koranic quotes, recitation of the 'tekbir'." And so on. And I'm going to miss -- I'm going to skip one part and go to the text again. It says: "The inaugural edition of 'El Mujahid' appeared thanks to the editorial work of Alija Izetbegovic, who was arrested shortly thereafter with his friend and co-conspirator Nazif Sacirbegovic." And then it goes on. It says there -- I'm going to skip a couple of lines. It says: "Izetbegovic admitted his membership in the Young Muslims and some of his conspiratorial activities, though he denied any personal cooperation with the Germans or membership in the Waffen-SS." And we see he -- that's -- he received a sentence. Now, this would have been the first time that Izetbegovic went to prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This spared him some later even stricter sentences. But you can find this in a book that a Muslim wrote about the Young Muslim organisation, and I've already presented all that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the second time that he was imprisoned, he was tried, in fact, by one of the lawyers who's appeared over here when she was a Prosecutor. He was convicted and he served time, and that would have been in the 1980s; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1983 onwards for five years, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, 1983 to about 1988. Now, if we go to page 40 of this document, which would be probably the next page for you, sir, at the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas. There may be a mistake in the transcript on line 9, page 28. You said that he was put in jail and he was tried -- no, he was defended by a lawyer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, no. The lawyer who is a Defence lawyer here was a prosecutor at the time. She prosecuted him, and as a result of the good work that she had done and the ample evidence, he was found guilty, and he served a sentence of five years. And, of course, it's not a secret that prosecutors eventually become or sometimes become defence lawyers, or vice versa, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was -- and I would prefer if we went into private session for that. That's why I didn't mention the name. But if you wished for me to put it on the record, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed in open session. We don't need the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at page 40 -- if we look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the light is on and it's red.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry for that. The "run" light says red, but the other one wasn't on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 40, and I believe I gave you the page number for you, sir, which is 1847, it says: "Beginning in the mid-1950s, the Young Muslims quietly re-absorbed members emerging from prison and re-established ties with the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt. The two secret societies were closely related, sharing an ideology and a conspiratorial milieu; the Bosnians had nothing but admiration for the Brotherhood, which had burrowed itself clandestinely throughout Egyptian society. Its motto summed up their ambition: 'The Koran is our constitution; the Prophet is our guide; death for the glory of Allah in our greatest ambition.' For their part, the Young Muslims had a similar slogan: 'Our path is jihad.' Under Izetbegovic's direction, the Sarajevo group maintained ties with the Brotherhood via secret meetings in several countries and, and arranged for contraband Islamic literature to be smuggled into Bosnia." Were you aware of that, General Praljak, that Izetbegovic during that period had not changed and was, in fact, pursuing his Young Muslim agenda?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I reads the "Islamic Declaration" as soon as it appeared and I studied it. That's number one. Number two, I know that Mr. Izetbegovic and his associates never gave up on that ideology. And, number three, before my very eyes during the war, something that we might call the Islamisation of the population and the military went from strength to strength. That world-view became more and more evident by the day, and that world-view was what was governing life in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I've already spoken about that. This was visible in the way they greeted each other and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go to page 44 of this document by Mr. Schindler, 1D00431. And for you, it would be 1850, the very last paragraph. Now we're moving up in history, and it says: "But the final straw was evidence of ties between the Young Muslims and Iran's revolutionary regime." And I think Mr. Schindler is talking about the same regime that we see on television today: "In the summer of 1982, Alija Izetbegovic and his long-time associate, Omer Behmen, who had served 11 years in Communist prisons for his service to the Islamic cause, proceeded to establish contacts with Tehran via the Iranian Embassy in Vienna, using a third Young Muslim, Teufik Velagic, and as a courier, Velagic's task was passing a copy of Izetbegovic's "Islamic Declaration," an unpublished manifesto of their movement that had been circulated underground in "samizdat" fashion. Apparently the Iranians liked what they saw, as they agreed to have the leadership of the Young Muslims visit Iran; they also arranged to meet with Bosnian Islamists in Abu Dhabi - a safer third country - to discuss mutual interests." And then further down on the same page, it says: "The best witness for the prosecution was the 'Islamic Declaration' which began with two maxims: 'Our objective: Islamisation of the world. Our motto is: To have faith and fight.'" "The unpublished book" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is Schindler's: "The unpublished book called for 'political revolution,' and stated without qualification, 'There can be no peace or harmony between 'Islamic religion' and non-Islamic social and institutions." Let me go on with this whole subject. We turn to page 48, and this is what Mr. Schindler says, and I'll ask you, since you told us that you've read the document. This is 1853. There is a section where Dr. Schindler has indicated: "That Izetbegovic was an Islamist could be doubted by none who read his writings with open eyes. The most damning indication of his mindset was the 'Islamic Declaration' which had been of interest to the secret police. Apparently written over years beginning in 1969, it was not completed until the early 1980s; it was not available to the public until its publication in Sarajevo in 1990, igniting a firestorm of controversy; a singularly odd manifesto, the 'Islamic Declaration' is a rambling document that never mentions Bosnia (that would have guaranteed immediate arrest by State Security), yet places Izetbegovic's religious-cum-political philosophy midstream in the Islamist current." And if with look at the next page, which is page 49, Dr. Schindler says, and this would be 1849 for you: "The reaction of the Bosnian Christians to such rhetoric was understandably immoderate. They viewed Izetbegovic's writing as 'a sort of Islamic "Mein Kampf."' In American terms, this would be tantamount to a white Southern politician who publicly extolled his slave-owning ancestors where running for office on a platform calling for return to ante-bellum values and practices. The opinions of African-Americans in such a scenario would be easy to predict, and rather like how non-Muslims in Bosnia viewed the rise of Izetbegovic." Now, you told us that you had read and studied this document. Do you have an opinion as to what Dr. Schindler is saying here and the reactions that he claims the Bosnian Christians - that's his term, that's not mine, and I suspect he's referring to the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Croats and the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Serbs - but can you comment a little bit on what Dr. Schindler is saying here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. What Mr. Schindler writes in his book, if I had been the one to tell him that in 1991, he would have proclaimed me a Croatian nationalist, as everybody else did, and therein lies the problem. The Americans could also read the "Islamic Declaration," and so did the French and the rest of them. Nobody knew anything at the beginning. They don't want to know, because they pursue ideas that have nothing whatsoever to do with reality, Mr. Karnavas. Nobody has ever studied thoroughly "Mein Kampf," nobody has ever understood "Mein Kampf," and that's why Hitler progressed. Nobody ever read this as they should. And I -- obviously the Americans, who imposed embargo, were pushing us towards Iran and allowed Iran to transport weapons via Croatia. I spoke with the minister of foreign affairs, Viran Galat [phoen], and I asked him why, why did this happen? Well, this is why: Nobody wanted to read anything, nobody wanted to make an effort to understand the situation. Every smart-ass comes and knows everything within the first 15 minutes, catastrophic moves and decisions are made, everything is then pushed into an abyss, and ten years later everybody is wise. And this is history, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's see what -- let's see what Dr. Schindler says about that, tying in what you just told us. Then I'm going to go back to the very beginning of this book and see how that might be able to help us a little bit. On page 201, page 201 of this document, 1D03137, and this would be page 1979 for you, 1979 for you, sir, it says: "Izetbegovic and his party succeeded in portraying this struggle as Western secular and democratic, when it was actually Eastern Islamic and authoritarian. Many Bosnian Muslims found the SDA vision acceptable or at least better than the other options, and weren't too troubled by Sarajevo's regular invocation of the jihad. For many, the SDA struggle had become theirs, and they confused the defence of Muslims with waging holy war, just as Izetbegovic wanted. "In a revealing interview, Hase Tiric, the commander of the Black Swans, a Muslim special-force unit that did its share of dirty work for the SDA during the war, was asked, 'Are you fighting for a Bosnia or a Muslim state?'" And his answer, according to this quote, is as follows: "What's the difference?" Did you know this gentleman, by the way, that's being quoted here, Tiric? Had you heard of him, and had you heard of the Black Swans?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of the Black Swans, and I know everything they did. And I also heard of the gentleman, although I don't know him. But we had complete, thorough information about the Black Swans. We knew what they were doing, how they were doing things, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that the Western media and some of the Western governments were rather naive in the way they behaved and what have you. Here we have a passage where we see Izetbegovic, how he's trying to portray his party. But let's look at page 15 of Dr. Schindler's book, 1D03137 for the record. That's page 15 in English, and I'll get you the number real quickly, but it's in Chapter 1, the very first page of Chapter 1 of the book, sir, the very first page of Chapter 1. We're going to go to Chapter 1 and -- it's 18 and 19, sir, I'm told. It starts with: "It was the achievement of a lifelong dream. As Adil Zulfikarpasic arrived at Velika Kladusa, in the northern --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it okay now? Okay. Let me begin -- start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's page 1825 for you, page 15 for us, document 1D03137: "The achievement of a lifelong dream. As Adil Zulfikarpasic arrived at Velika Kladusa in the north-western corner of Bosnia in mid-September 1990, he felt a pride and a hope he hadn't known since his youth." It then goes, further down, the next paragraph: "A devout Muslim, Zulfikarpasic was nevertheless a firm believer in secular politics and the need for Bosnian Muslims and Christians to coexist peacefully." Then the last paragraph: "It was therefore a shock for Zulfikarpasic to look out on the enormous crowd gathered, at least 300.000 people - some said as many as a half a million - in any event, it was the largest gathering of Muslims ever in Bosnia - and see among the party banners -- among the party banners deeply disturbing signs of jihadic [phoen]. There were over-sized banners in bright green, the colour of Islam; men adorned menacingly with sabres and turbans; shouts of 'Long live Saddam Hussein'; and, worst of all, banners and paearns [phoen] to Iran. "Zulfikarpasic turned to Alija Izetbegovic, the new party leader, who had recently been a political prisoner for advocating radical Islam, and pleaded for reason: 'By God, Alija, why are you doing this? Don't you know that in a half an hour, these pictures will be shown around the world?' Zulfikarpasic was terrified of giving ammunition to the enemies of Bosnia's Muslims. But Izetbegovic did not respond, even when Zulfikarpasic - the party's chief fundraiser and one of its three vice-presidents - admonished him, 'I don't want to participate in the slaughter of Muslims. Why do you have Khomeini's picture?'" That's the Ayatollah, not the recent -- not the Khamenei who's on now, but the old one: "Izetbegovic's non-response mystified and saddened the old man, who quickly concluded that the new party was leading his people to disaster. Two days later, he resigned his party posts and distanced himself from Izetbegovic and the party they had founded together. Zulfikarpasic said he found 'vast evidence of intolerance, religious exclusion, clerical meddling, and deceit.' Adil Zulfikarpasic hastily began a campaign trying to warn Bosnians that the party's programme and leadership were charting a road to ruin. No one listened." And my question to you, General Praljak, is: How is it possible for no one to have realised what Izetbegovic was up to, given that at a rally you have this sort of behaviour going on? How is it that the West didn't pick it up? Can you give us -- do you have any explanations for that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. First of all, you cannot say that no one understood, because I did, I understood, so please exclude me from saying this. A friend of mine, who is an academic, a Muslim - I won't mention his name now - I told him before the elections that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, those would not be a political elections, but simply a census. So the SDS would be the census for Serbs, HDZ for Croats, and SDA for Muslims. The results would correspond. All the assumptions that -- or catastrophic assumptions -- or, in fact, preparations for the catastrophe were in place, and every war is prepared ten years before it actually breaks out. Any serious observer or researcher is aware of it, but there are none left. No serious observers or researchers are not there. America created the al-Qaeda in Afghanistan to fight the Soviets. I simply can not understand the American policy. It is pursued -- they're running things as if it were a medium-size company, and they send out people who, in 15 minutes, learn more about the problem -- they know more than I do after 40 years of study, simply because they're Americans; America is the greatest power, the most powerful country in the world, and by dint of being an American, this person is the smartest person in the world. And in 15 minutes, and failing to understand anything, they make those catastrophic moves, and the war is a result. The war will definitely support further Islamisation, and if the people face extinction and killing, then they will turn to God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you're not really answering the question put to you by Mr. Karnavas, and you're extremely lengthy in your answer and wasting some of his time. But I have a follow-up question, however. Like everyone else, I took a look at this book, a book written by a person who seems to be a scholar. He is a lecturer at the American Naval Academy, and there are many sources to this book, notably expert from the OTP, Mr. Donia, as well as former analysts from the OTP, Attila Ohare [phoen], to mention him, who wrote a number of papers, including papers involving the documents sent by Serbia to the OTP. He's also basing his paper on sources coming from the CIA. So in this book, there are many things that are extremely interesting. And you just told Mr. Karnavas that you were one of those who had understood everything, but if you had understood that Mr. Izetbegovic, in his "Islamic Declaration" and with his troops, i.e., the Mujahedin, was leading a holy war, why is it that you supplied them with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, did you see how Croatia was blamed for everything, for putting a stop to the supply of weapons to -- or had we stopped supplying weapons to the Muslims, we would have been declared fascists, the worst kind of fascists and Ustashas in the world. Simply, it's prejudice, and once the world accepts that Muslims are victims because of what was going on in Sarajevo, and if you have somebody from America, from France, walking around there, if you told them something against the victim, if you tried to tell them that the victim is not as innocent as all that, Your Honours, they immediately branded you a criminal. In their opinion, the victim was unarmed, didn't do anything, there were no Mujahedin. There are truths that you cannot break down. It takes 15 years for the truths to come out, the truths that I knew. I knew impeccably the situation as it was developed, and the witnesses will say that in their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you just mentioned Sarajevo, but in this book the author mentions the gangs who were operating in Sarajevo; notably, the notorious Juka Prazina, as well as a well known Caco who were -- was pursuing ethnic cleansing, ethnic cleansing of Serbs. You were the deputy minister to defence, and you were also commander of the HVO at one point in time, so did you know all this, were you aware of all this; notably, what this Juka Prazina was up to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we knew everything. We knew about the executions that were going on. Well, hundreds of people were killed. Tens of thousands of people were expelled. Well, these were things that were an open secret. Well, aside for a large number of journalists, especially from UK -- well, please, don't talk to me about objective journalism. It doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you will continue, but I believe it's maybe time for a break, unless you have a quick question? No, a break? Let's break for 20 minutes, and then we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I believe that Mr. Ibrisimovic wanted the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. When Mr. Karnavas broached the topic as to who was a judge or a prosecutor in the Izetbegovic case, in the trial, I was involved in 1983, I was a lawyer in the law office that represented three of the accused. And this group of 13 people was convicted of verbal crime, thought crime, and the sentence that Mr. Izetbegovic received, nine years, was imposed by the Federal Court in Belgrade. I think that Mr. Praljak knows what the response was among the intellectuals, not only in Sarajevo, but in Belgrade and Zagreb, and that's all I had to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, I am aware of this response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Ibrisimovic. Mr. Karnavas, the Registrar told me that you have an hour and seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. And I wasn't aware that Mr. Ibrisimovic was involved. I knew that Edina Residovic, I as understand, was the prosecutor in the case, but that's my understanding of it, but we appreciate that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me pick up where the question from Judge Antonetti left us with, because the question was, How come the Croats were funnelling arms? If we look at Mr. Schindler's book, we also see that the Slovenians -- we also see that the Slovenians and -- were involved, and also that weapons were coming through Hungary. We also know that the Americans were involved, as you told us. So can you please explain to us, how is it that those countries, the neighbouring countries, first of all, got involved in breaking the arms embargo and funnelling weapons to the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and why is it that they didn't see that they were collaborating with extreme Islamic organisations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two reasons. The first reason was that a huge number of these people believed that Muslims were fighting the aggressors. And, secondly, because great sums of money were involved, and everybody was making a profit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I am referring to page 155 from Mr. Schindler's book, where he talks about this well-known organisation we heard here in this courtroom, TWRA, and he makes reference on that particular page about gun-running, and in particular he notes that by the summer of 1992, by the summer of 1992, Sarajevo had opened an arms corridor through Slovenia using ex-Soviet Bloc aircraft, 11-76 transports and MiG-26 helicopters to ferry Warsaw Pact weapons from Hungary to Bosnia through Slovenia airports. So here we have the neighbouring countries, who are also hosting some of the refugees, also involved in breaking the embargo and funnelling weapons into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of that, sir, at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just by serendipity, just to kind of this topic and then we'll move on, if we could look at a document that I just placed before everyone, and it's in the e-court, 1D03145, this is from the International Herald Tribune from yesterday, June 24, 2009. I happened to see it this morning, just by accident, but I think it might -- it ties in with Judge Antonetti's question and your answers. And it begins by saying, and I'll read slowly, the title is: "September 11 victims' families press lawsuit." "Documents gathered by lawyers for the families of September 11 victims provide new evidence of extensive financial support for al-Qaeda and other extremist groups by members of the Saudi royal family, but the material may never find its way into court because of legal and diplomatic obstacles." It goes on. At one point, it says: "Adding to the intrigue, classified American intelligence documents related to Saudi finances were leaked anonymously to lawyers for the families." A few lines down, it says: "The Saudis have long denied links to terrorists, and they have mounted an aggressive and so far successful campaign to beat back the allegations in federal court, based on a claim of sovereign immunity," not evidence, but just "sovereign immunity." "Saudi links to terrorism have been subject to years of government investigation and furious debate." The last paragraph of the first column: "A self-described al-Qaeda operative in Bosnia asserted in an interview with lawyers in the lawsuit that another charity, largely controlled by members of the royal family, the Saudi High Commission for Aid to Bosnia, provided money and supplies to the terrorist group in the 1990s and hired militant operatives like himself." And then one other passage I wish to read. The whole article is rather interesting, but one other passage, it says: "And a confidential German intelligence report gave a line-by-line description of tens of millions of dollars in bank transfers in the 1990s, with dates and dollar amounts, by Prince Salman bin Abdul-Aziz and other members of the Saudi royal family to another charity that was purportedly funding militants in Pakistan and Bosnia." Now, were you aware of this activity? That's my first question. And, secondly, since Alija Izetbegovic is being portrayed as the president of the Presidency for the entire country, and looking after the affairs of all those who are living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would include the Croats, can you please tell us whether you know, based on your position and experience, how much of the millions and millions of dollars being funnelled in by Saudis and others made its way to the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina who at the time were linked up with the Muslim forces at various times in fighting off the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that we had at the time, this involved hundreds of millions of dollars -- well, more than a billion dollars that were being funnelled in, we had no control mechanisms and we couldn't achieve that the Croats get anything from that money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go on, I just have one housekeeping matter, going back to the "Islamic Declaration," since we are moving it in as an exhibit, albeit up to date it has been declared as not relevant to these proceedings. So if we could look at 1D03142, 1D03142, this is an excerpt from a book that found its way in a footnote by none other than Mr. Tomljanovic, who is an OTP employee who testified here under the auspices of an expert, although as we know, he works for the Prosecution. Now, in this book by Mr. Suad Arnautovic, "Elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990" -- are you familiar with the book, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the individual, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, no, Suad Arnautovic, no, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, he does say in his book, and for us in English it would be -- if you look at the bottom pages, it would be 1832, it says: "Democratic Action Party was not directly publishing special publications, but the publisher of Sarajevo "Bosna" did publish a reprint of the book 'Islamic Declaration' written by Alija Izetbegovic. This edition was being advertised and distributed at the party gatherings and other events during the SDA election campaign." And it says: "Also, during the campaign, Fikret Abdic's book, 'My Response,' was being prepared and promoted during the campaign, and in early 1991 his other book, 'SDA, Will Do, Can Do and Know How to Do,' was also published." Now, again I want to make sure for the record, were you aware that this publication, the "Islamic Declaration," was being -- you told us it had been reprinted, but did you know it was actually being distributed at the SDA gatherings by none other than the president of the SDA during a period of time just preceding the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was published, I know that it was distributed. I'm not aware that Mr. Izetbegovic did the distributing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So now we can go back to where we were. If we go back to "The Unholy Terror."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, just an information. I do not see in the passage that it is said that Mr. Izetbegovic distributed the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's what -- exactly what General Praljak's indicated, that he did not distribute it. It was being distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he has it reprinted and it's being distributed. It's not -- how did it find its way to the party gathering? He never -- and as we've heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm -- excuse me. I am referring to page 44, lines 22 and following, where you asked Mr. Praljak: "Did you know it was actually being distributed by none other than the president of the SDA?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, I asked him, and we got his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, but you implied that it was distributed by the president of the SDA, and I wonder where the source of that knowledge of yours is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, my source is as follows, Your Honour: This is a party gathering. We saw the banners of Khomeini. He just gets out of prison, he republishes it. How did the copies get there? It's an assumption that I can make. You can reject it outright, and perhaps this is a way of trying to keep the document from being actually into evidence. But I dare say, we have ample evidence that he never renounces the "Islamic Declaration." It is being promoted. We have Zulfikarpasic, who is a devout Muslim, but nonetheless did not agree with Alija's policies, and I'm entitled to make -- to ask that question, and he provided the answer. The answer was he did not know of Izetbegovic actually distributing it. So you can take it or leave it as you wish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go back, because there seems to be doubts on the part of members of the Trial Chamber. Did Alija Izetbegovic, to your knowledge, ever renounce the "Islamic Declaration," and renounce those who were circulating it on his behalf, keeping in mind that he had been going to Iran, promoting it, meeting with the Ayatollah and the others in order to get funding from Iran, do you know of any instance where Alija Izetbegovic renounced his beliefs that he claims in the "Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A precise answer would be I don't know of any public place where Mr. Izetbegovic renounced the "Islamic Declaration."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he ever renounce anyone for distributing the publication; in other words, reproach them from circulating it, especially at political rallies, where he, as the president of the party, was trying to galvanize his party members to the party's agenda?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's look at page 52 of 1D03137. And for you, sir, it would be 1856, 1856. If we look at the very first paragraph, it says: "Abdic soon broke with the SDA. However, viewing it as a nest of Islamic radicalism, and Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic quit the party in disgust after the Velika Kladusa rally that revealed the ugly side of Izetbegovic's vision for Bosnia, Izetbegovic drove them out, purging them after they had been milked for money and respectability and were no longer needed. Abdic decided to run against Izetbegovic in the coming Bosnian presidential election, while Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic founded their own party, the Muslim Bosniak Organisation, to represent secular interests." This is the same Abdic that you were -- this is the same Abdic that you were questioned about at one point in time, I believe, by Judge Antonetti; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct as regards Abdic, and it is correct that Abdic's policy and Zulfikarpasic's policy and Filipovic's policy were different from the policy pursued by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go further down, lest there be any mistake, at least according to Mr. Schindler, he says, the following paragraph - I'll begin in the middle of it: "Bosnians were easily taken in by the SDA's bland declaration in defence of Muslim rights." And this is on page -- same page, 1857: "As one voter admitted, 'The SDA is the only party. I still don't know what their programme is, it's true. Somehow they don't say.' Of the 40 founders of the SDA, only 8 had been Young Muslims, but those veterans, Izetbegovic's trusted cabal, ran the party from its foundation. They mostly held key posts behind the scenes, serving as the movement's 'untouchable core.'" We go on, we'll skip a couple of lines: "What the party looked like had been explained in the 'Islamic Declaration,' 'The struggle for an Islamic system and a thorough rebuilding of Muslim society can only be successfully carried out by hardened personalities, forming a strong and homogeneous organisation. This organisation is not a political party from the arsenal of Western democracy; it is a movement based on Islamic theology.' In a rare moment of candour, Izetbegovic admitted that the role of the Young Muslims was vital. 'The fact is that a huge number of those people, most of them participated in the creation of the SDA in 1990.'" And just to make sure that we have it right, is this fellow -- Omer Behmen, was he a Young Muslim, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move to page 54, let's stay with page 53. Mr. Karnavas said something earlier, Mr. Praljak. He said Mr. Abdic had had more votes than Mr. Izetbegovic, and I was quite interested by this. If Abdic has more votes, why is it that he is not head of the party, head of the Presidency?
